| [DR-1079](DR-1079-nineteen-collisions-in-seven-days.md) | **Nineteen collisions in seven days — the next number is the next FREE number.** DR-1021's own `re-review: 2026-10-21`, run five days early on its own condition (*"count the week's collisions; if the rate holds, that convention is the next conversation"*). MEASURED: **19 renumber events in 7 days**, about 2.7 a day — not an edge case being monitored but the normal operating condition of a repo with concurrent sessions. Today's was the fifth: lesson 248 moved DR-1072→DR-1074 because my own pair took 1072 and 1073 while that branch sat in CI. WHY IT HAPPENS, EXACTLY: `**Next ID:**` is one shared line and the resolver computes it as `maxRowId(INDEX) + 1` — **from what is on disk**; two sessions branching off the same main both read the same number and both take it, and neither did anything wrong, because the number really was free when each looked. Disk cannot see a branch that has not landed. SO THE QUESTION IS WIDENED AND NOTHING ELSE CHANGES: from *"what is free on disk?"* to *"what is free on disk AND not already claimed by a branch still in flight?"* `**Next ID:**` stays one line, the resolver still owns it and still computes from disk, DR-0644's refusal still refuses, no past record moves, no citation changes. Unmerged branches ONLY — a merged branch's files are already in main so `maxRowId` counted them, which is what keeps the scan small: **892 branches** in this repo, a handful in flight, further bounded to the 60 most recently touched refs. It decides nothing and writes nothing: it reports the lowest free number and NAMES the branch holding each number it steps over, leaving the resolver the only thing that writes the pointer (two things computing one line is how they drift — DR-1021's own reason for leaving the pointer alone). AND IT CAUGHT A LIVE ONE ON ITS FIRST REAL RUN: `DR-1076 — origin/ccr-9c70f297-ct1dox` — **this record's own number, already claimed by another branch**, which the pointer would have handed over. It keeps 1076 deliberately: that branch has not landed, and a record about collisions that quietly dodged one would teach the wrong thing. 10 cases weighted at what must NOT count as a claim (INDEX.md names every number there has ever been, so reading it as claims would make every number look taken; README/PRINCIPLES likewise; a DR in prose is not a file claim; three- and five-digit numbers are not records) and at never returning BELOW the pointer, since reusing a retired number points every existing citation at the wrong record. Proven to catch twice — ignoring what branches hold fails both step-over cases; loosening the path match so INDEX.md counts fails two more — file restored byte-identical after each; and proven on the LIVE repo (976 records read, a real branch found) which a fixture cannot do. NOT the convention change DR-1021 reserved for the Governor (that one touches every past record); this is additive, read-only, reversible by deleting one file. NOT wired into the lane on purpose — DR-1021's reasoning holds that a renumber inside a merge step is where a mistake is least visible. Does not stop two sessions that both run it in the same minute before either pushes; only a shared reservation can, and that is the reserved change. `re-review: 2026-10-23` — read next week's renumber count; if it does not fall, the next move is the lane running this before a decision file is written. | accepted | A | the decision ledger | VERIFICATION-DOCTRINE, DECISION-RECORDS, PERPETUAL-IMPROVEMENT |

HONEST ABOUT THE NOTICE IT CANNOT GIVE: the calendar's longest lead is one month and insurance wants sixty days, so `noticeGapDays` states the difference instead of quietly under-warning. INTEGRATED, because he had to say so: `DocumentRenewals` renders inside the Legal shelf over its own and the household's documents and the shell hands it the real `addEvent`, so a confirmed renewal becomes an event that really notifies — three libraries shipped with no caller today (DR-1072, DR-1073, measured again in DR-1075) and this one is wired in the same change. 27 cases weighted at what misleads about a document that matters, including an insurance DISPUTE not being mistaken for a POLICY (both real entries in LEGAL_CATEGORIES, only one has a renewal date); proven to catch by three mutations — undated reading as valid (3 fail), unknown assumed permanent (2 fail), a re-deduction overwriting the person's date (2 fail) — restored byte-identical after each; reminder keys asserted to be ones REMINDER_OPTIONS actually has, since an invented key is silently skipped and nobody is ever told; leap years and month-end clamping pinned. Reading it to settle the question found a hazard nobody had hit: the old form streamed the first attempt's stdout straight out and let the retry print the same rows again, so a docker dying PART WAY through a result set handed its caller a doubled answer with exit 0 -- and when both attempts failed it emitted the half-written rows as data. ON_ERROR_STOP=1 and the exit-code contract are untouched and pinned. Verified: 10 cases that lift the QUOTED heredoc out and run it against stub docker/sudo -- no NAS, no network; proven-to-catch twice, including reverting to main's version and measuring 6 of 10 red, so the hazard is confirmed present on main rather than reasoned about. FIX: split an unbalanced tail on its `(DR-NNNN = ` markers (the balanced path is byte-identical, so well-formed input is unchanged) and dedupe the first list against itself. Plus a one-time repair with the tool's own functions: line 950 25,721,382 -> 41,091 chars, the file 27,573,001 -> 1,670,097 bytes, line count unchanged at 1,265, every other line byte-identical, all 34 distinct segments preserved. (Stale PR titles — #2298 said DR-1129 — are noise; the FILE is the claim.) MEASURED at `e8fc20407`: guard FAIL real exit 1; 2 records on 1131; pointer DR-1133; **17 bare `DR-1131` citations across 13 files the renumber tool REFUSED to rewrite, 6 of which meant the record that would have STAYED** — a blind sweep would have mis-cited three sov43 artifacts. **TWO MEASUREMENT ERRORS OF MINE.** (1) I read a failing guard as PASSING: piped through `tail`, the shell reported `EXIT=0` — the pipeline’s status, not the guard’s; without the pipe it is 1. **A guard read through a pipe can look green while failing.** (2) I measured `main` once and then acted for forty minutes as though it had not moved — it had. DECIDED: **the instance was already fixed on `main` by ANOTHER SESSION (#2303, `3d345746c`) and that resolution stands** — DR-1131 the voice witness STAYED, DR-1133 is a new research-tier record, DR-1134 is sov43 MOVED, pointer DR-1135. **My own fix was about to be the third collision:** off the red `main` I had moved the OPPOSITE record (the voice witness → DR-1133) and taken DR-1134 for this record, and both numbers now belong to DIFFERENT decisions on `main`; merging my repair would have re-broken the exact thing it repaired, with TWO duplicates instead of one. The failure recurred INSIDE the fix for it, on a green branch, in under an hour — nothing in that branch was wrong when written; `main` simply moved, which is the whole shape of the defect. So the branch was reset onto `3d345746c` and every rename and citation edit DROPPED, keeping only this record: where another session’s repair is merged and green, **the second repair yields** (DR-0644 refuses rather than folds precisely because two plausible repairs of one collision can each destroy the other’s). WHAT IS GAINED: their commit fixed the instance; nothing recorded why no gate could have stopped it, that MERGE ORDER is the only tiebreak both sides agree on, or that a second repair yields to a merged one. **WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, with a why and a date:** it does not PREVENT the next collision. The check is nameable — refuse a PR whose new number is already claimed by `main` or another OPEN PR — but it needs the open-PR list at CI time (token, rate limits, fork behaviour) IN THE MERGE LANE, and DR-0107 forbids a lane change without proving the deploy; coupling that to a one-file record is the wrong trade. **`re-review: 2026-10-27`** — build it or say why not. Measured cost it would have saved today: one red `main`, two competing repairs, a renumber on a third branch. Verified: guard on `3d345746c` OK (newest DR-1134, pointer correct) read WITHOUT a pipe; with this record and the pointer at DR-1137, guard OK, lint exit 0, verify:gates exit 0, decision-chain green. Independent of my account (DR-0076 §7): `git ls-tree origin/main docs/decisions/` lists their three files and the pointer itself; restoring a second DR-1131 row reproduces the same sentence and exit 1. The limit plainly: nothing here makes a collision impossible, and this record does not claim otherwise — it makes it cheap, loud and recoverable, says WHO YIELDS when two repairs race, and dates the check that would make it impossible. |

MEASURED by the instrument itself at `3d345746c`: **116 jobs total**, 115 enabled, **1 disabled** (`openers`, the garage-door service, shipped off on purpose); 87 workflow files + 29 NAS services; **65 scheduled, 40 ON-DEMAND ONLY, 11 event-driven, 0 inert**; last-run **not measurable from a checkout** — so every job reads UNKNOWN **in those words**, never a zero that would look like “none have run”. The **40 on-demand-only workflows are his second question in our own fleet** (`inbox-lesson-body`, `rls-isolation`, `nas-bootstrap`, `cams-diag` and 36 more): in a report of that shape all 40 appear as “enabled, no last run date” and all 40 are fine. DECIDED: `lastRunClass()` returns exactly one of ran/never/unknown and returns **never ONLY when the history was asked and answered zero** — a missing entry or a failed lookup is unknown (pinned five ways, incl. that the three are disjoint over every input shape). `triggersOf()` matches only TOP-LEVEL `on:` keys, so a cron in a comment or under a job is not a schedule — a false “scheduled” would hide the one alarming class, a job nothing fires. GitHub’s own `disabled_manually`/`disabled_inactivity` beats the file’s existence. The asking half `fleet-census.yml` is **read-only** (`contents: read`), mutates nothing, PAGINATES the whole workflow list, uses each workflow’s exact `total_count` rather than inferring from an empty page, and prints the **retention caveat with the verdict** (“never” = no run in RETAINED history, not “never once fired”); brakes: one pass, 10-min ceiling, one run at a time, weekly off the hour. “Disabled” is reported with the job’s own stated purpose, never as a verdict — disabled alone cannot tell *seasonal* from *staged* from *dead*; the description can. **NOT DONE, with a why and a date:** no in-app surface yet, and DR-0065 says that is where it belongs — the data file is the prerequisite and lands here. The NAS and routine fleets’ last-run is read today by `loops-health.yml` and the routine API but not yet folded into this census; the script already takes it as INPUT, so folding it in is data, not code. **`re-review: 2026-11-03`** for both. **THE CENSUS GOT A REAL CONSUMER BECAUSE A GATE REFUSED IT TWICE:** `interconnect-guard` (DR-0621) rejected the workflow first for having no place in the flow graph, then for reading a resource nobody writes — both right. A census whose output lands only in a step summary is the hollow kind, so it now files the TWO genuinely broken classes on the rolling ledger the OpsBoard already reads: a job **nothing can fire at all**, and a job something fires **on a clock** with no run in retained history. It files NEITHER “on-demand with no runs” (nothing is meant to fire it) NOR “unknown” (a gap in the report, not a fault in the job) — a case pins that the filter contains neither. And **GitHub writes `gh:actions-fleet`, not us** (the API is the only place a workflow’s disabled state and retained run count exist), so it is declared an outside source with that reason. Verified: 20 cases; `fleet-census.yml` parses, both shell steps pass `bash -n`, embedded python compiles, the github-script body passes `node --check`; lint and verify:gates exit 0 read WITHOUT a pipe. Proven to catch: letting unknown fall through to never turns **3** red (*“expected ‘never’ to be ‘unknown’”*, *“expected 88 to be +0”*); widening the trigger match so a commented-out cron counts turns **1** red. **AN ERROR INSIDE MY OWN VERIFICATION, recorded because it is today’s shape again:** my first break-and-restore pass ran the test through a shell function that `cd`-ed into `app/`, so the restoring `cp` hit a relative path that no longer existed — the “restored” run printed the SAME three failures as the break, and the second break’s run printed them too, so one break was never tested and the restore never happened. The tell was three identical outputs in a row. Re-done with absolute paths: break 1 red on 3, break 2 red on 1, restored 18 passed. **A verification harness can fail in a way that makes every reading identical, and identical readings are the tell.** |

| [DR-1151](DR-1151-the-census-asks-the-loops.md) | **The census asks the loops -- 28 blank columns were a missing argument, not a missing road.** DR-1148 shipped the fleet census with 28 of 118 rows blank, stated the NAS limitation honestly, and dated it `re-review: 2026-11-20` on the grounds that folding those histories in is "data, not code". READING THE CODE SAYS OTHERWISE: `readServices()` hardcoded `lastRunClass: 'unknown'` with the comment "loops-health.yml reads them; it is not in the repo" -- true of the REPO, false of the FLEET. `loops-health.yml` already measures all 29 loops on the tailnet every fifteen minutes (a per-loop verdict ok/failed/degraded/unknown, the services-sync clock's last fire, each loop's own ledger age), and `readServices()` simply never accepted the `runs` argument. A PARAMETER NEVER PASSED, not a measurement nobody could take -- the DR-0108 failure exactly: reasoning from my own reach (this sandbox cannot touch the NAS) instead of the team's (a runner does it every quarter hour). DECIDED, one road to one truth: loops-health PUBLISHES the witness it already builds onto the same rolling report-issue road DR-1148 established (`loops-report`, deliberately NOT `incident`), and the census READS it GitHub-side with no tailnet of its own -- no second NAS reader, because two roads to one truth drift and the loop witness owns what a loop's last run means (DR-0621). Publishing CANNOT change the witness's verdict: the step runs after the verdict and carries `continue-on-error: true`, so a healthy witness never goes red because an issue write failed and a dark one never goes green. WHICH WITNESS SAID SO travels with the timestamp: a loop's own ledger age wins (it is that loop's file), the services-sync clock is the fallback and only for a loop whose last run that cycle was `ok`, anything else stays null, and each entry carries `from` in words. | [DR-1161](DR-1161-the-witness-cannot-fail-in-silence.md) | **The witness cannot fail in silence -- a brake that turns a failure into a green is a disarmed check.** DR-1152 fixed a fabricated timestamp and, in the same commit, stopped the loops witness publishing at all; for TWO HOURS nothing said so. MEASURED 2026-10-21 on the live repository: NINE collisions landed on main in eleven hours; FIVE numbers taken by other sessions in one hour (1153-1157); and at 05:30 THREE open PRs racing on TWO numbers -- #2338 and #2340 both introducing DR-1158, #2339 and #2340 both introducing DR-1159. Every one of those checks had already run and classified the race correctly, and NOT ONE SIDE HAD BEEN TOLD. One was this author's; one was a lesson whose number I had assigned an hour earlier and had to correct mid-build when another session took it. DR-1147 dated this question for 2026-11-03; the answer came thirteen days early and it was no. DECIDED: the contested verdict is detected from the READER'S OWN OUTPUT (grep for `CONTESTED WITH AN OPEN PR` in the text it already printed -- a second computation could disagree with the verdict it reports); a contested PR gets ONE comment, created once and updated after, saying in words that nobody has lost the race, that the check does not fail on it, that whichever merges second has to move (DR-1136), and that the rename belongs on a CLEAN tree because mid-merge two records hold the number and every bare citation becomes ambiguous; each racing PR runs the check itself, so one comment per PR reaches every side with no cross-posting and no central notifier to keep alive. DELIBERATELY UNCHANGED: the only thing that may fail this check is still `taken-on-main` -- a race still cannot block a PR, which is the split that let DR-1147 ship with three lesson branches in flight. The repair moves from AFTER the merge to BEFORE it, which is where it is cheap: a rename on a clean tree is one command and the tool rewrites every citing file, while the same rename found after a second merge costs a red main, an aborted merge, bare citations read one at a time and a re-verify. THIS DOES NOT PREVENT A COLLISION and does not claim to -- two PRs opened minutes apart can still both claim a free number; this only ensures both know. Prevention needs a CLAIM-TIME RESERVATION (a number taken by writing to a shared registry before the record is written), which alters how every session authors a record and which all 1,059 existing records depend on; DR-1021 recorded that as a Governor's decision rather than a tooling change and it stays one -- but its evidence now lives in a record instead of an argument. `re-review: 2026-10-28` to count the week's collisions again with both sides warned. 22 cases (5 new); three PROVEN TO CATCH by breaking the workflow: the contested comment made to call setFailed -> 1 red; a new comment every push instead of one updated -> 1 red; the flag computed from something other than the reader's output -> 1 red; restored 22 passed each time, and a fourth case pins that taken-on-main still fails with exit 1. | [DR-1177](DR-1177-another-tenants-hallway-is-not-this-tenants-door.md) | **Another tenant's hallway is not this tenant's door -- the pre-ticked suggestion stops offering the whole building.** Darrell asked it straight mid-build, 2026-10-21: "Tenants only get their door right?" The right answer was YES BY MECHANISM AND NO BY DEFAULT, and only a measurement could tell them apart. By mechanism yes: a grant names its cameras, the NAS returns only those on `/list` and answers `403 not-your-camera` for any other ticket (`cams_forwarder.py:4061`, proven in the service's own self-test at `:5255-5260`). MEASURED by running the real function before any change: 805 Prospect Apt 1 and Apt 2 arrived pre-ticked with IDENTICAL sets, the neighbour's hallway in both; `expect(apt1).toEqual(apt2)` ran green and so did `expect(apt1).toContain('805_apt2_hallway')`. Another PROPERTY's cameras were correctly excluded (`1313_porch` never appeared), so the address matching worked -- the unit was simply never part of it. NOTHING LEAKED BY ITSELF: the NAS enforced exactly what each grant named and the landlord's ticks were always the real gate. What could leak was a landlord pressing Share without unticking -- and the whole point of pre-ticking is that it is usually right, so it is usually pressed. DECIDED: a camera marked for a DIFFERENT unit is no longer pre-ticked. `unitOf()` reads a unit only where it is MARKED (`apt 2`, `unit B`, `#3`, `suite 101`), so the house number in "805 porch floodlight" is never mistaken for a unit and a common-area camera stays common; `doorUnit()` reads the door's own label the same way, falling back to its trailing token so a bare `B` still reads as unit `b`. COMMON CAMERAS ARE UNTOUCHED -- porch, back door, lot, anything unmarked -- because those are what a household is normally given, and the porch is the one he has asked for since 2026-10-09. A WHOLE HOUSE NARROWS NOTHING: no unit label means no unit to be another's. THIS CHANGES WHAT IS OFFERED, NEVER WHAT IS ALLOWED -- the landlord can still tick anything by hand, the NAS's permission rule is entirely unchanged, and the owner stays the one who decides (DR-0841); pinned as its own case so a later reader does not mistake it for a permission boundary. 6 new cases, one PROVEN TO CATCH: `notAnothersUnit(c)` removed from the filter (the old behaviour exactly) -> 1 red; restored 23 passed, and the existing DR-0841 suite stayed green at 14. NOT CLOSED: IT HAS NOT RUN YET -- the next firing is its first real exercise and the log's first line is the proof, `re-review: 2026-10-22`; it does not fix the Actions-listing cost, which is a tool behaviour in this session and not the repository's, it ROUTES AROUND it, which is the DR-0108 move (a stated "can't" is a premise to challenge, and the answer was that six existing witnesses had already built the road); and the builder-progress step is untouched, its output still only in the step summary, `re-review: 2026-11-04`. THE GATES CAUGHT A PREMISE ERROR IN THIS RECORD'S OWN DESIGN: `issues: write` was added without checking whether anything already guaranteed its absence, and `lesson-inbox-bell.test.js:247` had asserted since before this work that this workflow carries NO `issues: write | pull-requests: write | contents: write` -- so two tests in one suite flatly contradicted each other and shard 1/4 failed, correctly.
